questions.q: Which of the following instruments is primarily used in chain surveying to mark the exact end of a chain length and to help keep a tally of the total number of chains measured on the ground?
questions.explain: **Chaining arrows** (or pins) are metal skewers inserted into the ground to mark the end of each chain or tape length during a measurement. The follower collects them, and counting the collected arrows helps keep tally of the total distance measured. **Ranging poles** are used to establish straight lines, while a **cross staff** is used to set out right angles.

questions.q: When plotting a closed compass traverse on paper, it is common to find that the final drawn line fails to perfectly meet the original starting point due to cumulative field measurement inaccuracies. This gap is known in surveying as the:
questions.explain: A **closing error** occurs in a closed traverse when the plotted endpoint does not coincide with the starting point. This discrepancy results from minor inaccuracies in measuring angles (bearings) and distances during fieldwork, and it is usually distributed and corrected graphically (for example, using the Bowditch rule).

questions.q: During field surveying, surveyors must often employ geometric techniques to avoid obstacles on the survey line. Which of the following features represents an obstacle to *chaining* but NOT to *ranging*?
questions.explain: In elementary surveying, obstacles are classified based on what they obstruct. A **wide flowing river** prevents a surveyor from physically stretching a chain or tape directly across the ground (obstacle to chaining), but it does not block the line of sight to align ranging poles on the opposite bank (no obstacle to ranging). A tall building or a dense forest obstructs *both* chaining and ranging.
